newsitem.title: GERMANY: Lamfalussy says choice of EMU entrants very hard.
newsitem.headline: Lamfalussy says choice of EMU entrants very hard.

text.p: Alexandre Lamfalussy, the head of the European Monetary Institute, said on Monday that the 1998 decision on which nations qualified for European monetary union would be an extremely difficult one for all concerned.

Even leaving aside political issues, it would be very hard to assess which countries met the criteria laid down in the Maastricht Treaty in a lasting, sustainable way, Lamfalussy told Frankfurt's International Business Journalists Forum.

He noted that the Maastricht Treaty -- which lays down the economic conditions countries must meet to join the single currency in 1999 -- has very clearly-defined targets on some of its criteria and deliberately leaves verbal scope on others.

"The Maastricht Treaty is quite explicit about some criteria, but less clear on others," the head of the EMI, the forerunner to the European Central Bank, said. The EMI has an advisory function in determining which countries will take part in the Euro launch.

Referring in particular to the condition most countries are findiing hardest to meet -- the need to cut budget deficits -- he added: "The exceptions are defined in words not in figures. The word sustainability is used very heavily."
This meant that the assessment of which countries had made the EMU grade was "professionally a very difficult task to carry out," he added.

The clauses in the Maastricht Treaty that call for public deficits of would-be EMU member countries to be no more than three percent of gross domestic product and borrowing to total less than 60 percent of GDP have sub-clauses that permit countries to overshoot the criteria in exceptional economic circumstances.
The decision on who has made the EMU grade is to be made in March or April 1998 on the basis of actual data from 1997.
Regarding the issue of which countries should be selected for monetary union, Lamfalussy said the question was not one of quantity, but rather of quality.
"I am in favour neither of large or small, but of a safe group in the beginning," he said.

Declining to respond directly to a question as to whether or not European integration was facing worrying trends -- with debt rising in Europe's largest economy, Germany, and budgets still out of control in other countries, Lamfalussy said it was clear that worries about qualification were gaining strength now.
"It is natural that approaching difficult dates and decisions you get a lot of agitation," he said. "This is one of the most crucial decisions that will have been made."
Lamfalussy added that a growing perception the EMU will actually happen, as planned in 1999, was feeding into this concern.
"The debate is there now because it becomes a genuine reality," he said.
